# Projection-normalized layer-cake lattice discrepancy

These are uniform sampling inequalities. They do not locate a mixed
center and do not prove OC. Their error depends on the geometry of
the projection onto the sampled variables, rather than the total
coarse volume or the thickness in the continuous variables.

## 1. Absolute inequality with the exact peak fiber volume

Let r>=1 and s>=0. Let Q be a compact convex subset of
R^r_u times R^s_x. Its projection P is assumed contained in
[-R,R]^r, R>0. Let L+a be a full-rank lattice coset in R^r with
covolume v and measurable cells contained in [-delta,delta]^r.
Set

    f(u)=vol_s(Q_u),         F=max_u f(u),
    M=vol_(r+s)(Q),
    mu(A)=v sum_(lambda in L+a) vol_s((Q intersect A)_lambda).

For s=0, f is the indicator of P and F is one when Q is nonempty,
zero otherwise. Empty Q is allowed. For every closed ambient
halfspace H, as well as for H equal to the entire space,

    |mu(H)-vol_(r+s)(Q intersect H)|
       <= 2r delta(2R+2delta)^(r-1) F.                  (1)

No full-dimensionality or zero-boundary-mass assumption is needed.

For s>=1, f is bounded and upper semicontinuous. To check the latter,
if u_j->u then all limit points of the compact bounded sections Q_u_j
lie in Q_u. Thus for every epsilon>0 those sections eventually lie
in the epsilon-neighborhood of Q_u in R^s. Taking volumes and then
decreasing epsilon gives limsup f(u_j)<=f(u). Consequently its
positive superlevel sets {u:f(u)>=t}, t>0, are compact. They are
convex by Brunn--Minkowski on the sections; the same facts apply to
the section-volume function f_H of Q intersect H. Its peak is at
most F, and all its superlevel sets lie in [-R,R]^r.

The elementary lattice-count version of the cell discrepancy lemma
in `candidate 0639bd50a01557c4`
states that for every compact convex A subset [-R,R]^r,

    |v #(A intersect (L+a))-vol_r(A)|
        <=2r delta(2R+2delta)^(r-1).                    (2)

Apply (2) to {f_H>=t}, and integrate 0<t<F. Tonelli's theorem
identifies the two integrals as v sum_lambda f_H(lambda) and
integral f_H. Values at a single threshold do not affect this
identity, so closed superlevels retain every sampled boundary value.
The triangle inequality under the integral proves (1). For s=0,
(1) is directly (2) applied to Q intersect H.

## 2. Peak versus total volume

Suppose M>0 and s>=1. Then P has positive r-volume and F>0. Choose
u0 with f(u0)=F. For 0<=theta<=1, root-concavity of f gives

    f((1-theta)u0+theta u) >= (1-theta)^s F,
       u in P.

Thus, for 0<t<F, the t-superlevel set contains the homothetic copy

    u0+(1-(t/F)^(1/s))(P-u0).

Layer cake now gives

    M >= F vol_r(P) integral_0^1 (1-a^(1/s))^r da
      = F vol_r(P) / binom(r+s,r).                     (3)

For the integral, the substitution b=a^(1/s) gives
s integral_0^1 b^(s-1)(1-b)^r db=s! r!/(r+s)!, by repeated
integration by parts. For s=0, (3) holds as equality M=vol_r(P)
with F=1 and binom(r,r)=1.

Combining (1) and (3), for every closed H,

    |mu(H)-vol_(r+s)(Q intersect H)|/M
       <= binom(r+s,r)
          *2r delta(2R+2delta)^(r-1)/vol_r(P).            (4)

The denominator in (4) is the projection volume. A small continuous
fiber height, a varying slope in x, or a small total M does not by
itself worsen this relative estimate.

## 3. Normalize only the sampled projection

For full-dimensional P, choose an affine normalization u'=Au+b
such that

    B_2^r subset AP+b subset R_r B_2^r,
    R_r=r(r+2).

The maximal-inscribed-simplex construction proves this elementary
normalization. Leave x unchanged. The transformed fine lattice is
A(L+a)+b and its covolume is |det A|v. Both its sampled weighted
mass and the full coarse volume acquire the SAME factor |det A|.
Hence normalized halfspace masses and depths are unaffected by this
base-only affine change; arbitrary oblique halfspaces transform to
arbitrary oblique halfspaces.

If the transformed lattice has a cell in [-eta,eta]^r, then (4)
in these coordinates gives

    sup_H |mu(H)-vol_(r+s)(Q intersect H)|/M
       <= e(r,s,eta)
        := [2r binom(r+s,r)/kappa_r]
             eta(2R_r+2eta)^(r-1).                     (5)

The same inequality holds for total mass. If e<1, normalization by
the actual sampled total yields

    sup_H |mu(H)/mu(total)-vol_(r+s)(Q intersect H)/M|
          <=2e/(1-e).                                  (6)

In particular the sampled total is positive. The transformed
covering radius tending to zero is sufficient, since Voronoi cells
can be assigned their null boundaries and placed inside cubes of
that radius.

## 4. Several coarse fibers may use different projection maps

Let a finite family Q_z have positive full coarse volumes M_z and
actual common sampled lattice L+a in the u variables. For EACH z
one may use a different base-only projection normalization A_z.
It is being used to estimate a scalar discrepancy for that fiber,
not as a claimed global transformation of the mixed set.

If eta_z are the corresponding transformed cell bounds, (5) gives
for every ORIGINAL closed ambient halfspace H

    |mu_z(H)-nu_z(H)|<=e(r,s,eta_z) M_z.

Indeed its restriction to fiber z is a halfspace in (u,x), and
the base-only transformation remains affine on that individual
fiber. Undoing the determinant factor gives the displayed inequality
in the original measure. Summing yields

    sup_H |sum_z mu_z(H)-sum_z nu_z(H)|/sum_z M_z
       <= sum_z e(r,s,eta_z) M_z / sum_z M_z.             (7)

Thus if every eta_z tends to zero, the normalized fine and coarse
halfspace masses converge uniformly, regardless of the total coarse
volume scale. With 0<sum_z M_z<infinity, the same numerical estimate
also holds for a countable family and a uniform error bound tending
to zero, by absolute summability. No infinite-family center or
compactness conclusion is asserted.

If a coarse fiber has M_z=0, (1) still controls its sampled mass
absolutely, but (4)--(7) do not turn that into a relative-volume
bound for that fiber. Such a fiber can carry positive fine measure.
It must be retained in an absolute error estimate, or its negligible
fine mass must be separately proved before deleting it.

Finally, uniform cap discrepancy alone does not put a coarse center
on the sampled lattice. Feasible recovery is a separate geometric
step, supplied only under the hypotheses of the compact-lift recovery
theorems. No rounding step is implicit in (5)--(7).
